A_target.statement:
Let $X$ be a [[Definition:Topological Space|topological space]].
Then the set of [[Definition:Path Component|path components]] is:
:$\map {\pi_0} X = X / \sim$
where $x \sim y$ {{iff}} there is a [[Definition:Path (Topology)|path]] from $x$ to $y$, and a mapping out of $\map {\pi_0} X$ is well-defined {{iff}} it is constant along paths.

B_source.statement:
Let $\sim$ be an [[Definition:Equivalence Relation|equivalence relation]] on a set $X$.
Then mappings $X / \sim \to Y$ correspond to mappings $X \to Y$ constant on each [[Definition:Equivalence Class|equivalence class]].

substitutions.the equivalence relation: the relation of being joined by a path
substitutions.the classes of the relation: the path components of the space

derived.the induced map on the quotient: the well-defined map on path components

validity_conditions: Being joined by a path is an equivalence relation: constant paths give reflexivity, reversal gives symmetry, and concatenation gives transitivity.
A map is constant on classes exactly when it is constant along every path, which is the descent condition.
For a continuous map into a discrete space this is automatic on each path component, which is why path components detect exactly the locally constant functions.
proof_plan:
Define $x \sim y$ {{iff}} there is a path $\gamma: \closedint 0 1 \to X$ with $\map \gamma 0 = x$ and $\map \gamma 1 = y$.
Constant paths, reversed paths and concatenated paths show $\sim$ is an [[Definition:Equivalence Relation|equivalence relation]].
By the source result, mappings out of $\map {\pi_0} X$ correspond to mappings on $X$ constant along paths.
